explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Asaph, whose name is on this psalm, asks, “Why does Your anger smolder against the sheep of Your pasture?” (Psalm 74:1) Sheep are not exactly the toughest creatures on the farm. I think that makes the question hit even softer.

Close on the farm theme, baker, but there's no vineyard in this verse. Asaph says, “Why does Your anger smolder against the sheep of Your pasture?” (Psalm 74:1) The people are sheep and the setting is a pasture. Nobody's pruning anything in this verse.

Stones come up later in the psalm's ruins, friend, but not here. Asaph calls the people “the sheep of Your pasture.” (Psalm 74:1) Stones sit there and sheep need looking after. I think that's why the question stings.
Zion it is, friend. Asaph says it plainly: “Mount Zion, where You dwell.” (Psalm 74:2) He's pointing God right back to His own address. Hard to say it's the wrong house when the mail goes there.

Sinai is a famous mountain, baker, but Asaph doesn't name it here. He says, “Mount Zion, where You dwell.” (Psalm 74:2) This prayer is about the place where God dwells and where the ruins are. Zion is the name on this one.

Nice mountain pick, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. Asaph asks God to remember “Mount Zion, where You dwell.” (Psalm 74:2) That's the mountain he has on his heart. Carmel will have to wait for another passage.

I get why that sounds right, baker, but listen to what Asaph asks. He wants God to look at “everything in the sanctuary the enemy has destroyed.” (Psalm 74:3) Everything, not a few things. This was no scuffed corner or loose hinge.

False is right, friend. Asaph asks God to turn His steps to “everything in the sanctuary the enemy has destroyed.” (Psalm 74:3) He's not listing a couple of dents. He says everything, and he calls it everlasting ruins.
Yep, baker. The foes were “smashing all the carvings with hatchets and picks.” (Psalm 74:6) All of them, not just the ones in the front. Tools like that are made for a job, and this was a sad one.

Good guess, but the psalm doesn't mention basins. Asaph says they were “smashing all the carvings with hatchets and picks.” (Psalm 74:6) The carvings are what get smashed here. Sometimes the answer is the plain thing in the verse, friend.

The altar doesn't show up in these verses, friend. Asaph says the foes were “smashing all the carvings with hatchets and picks.” (Psalm 74:6) Carvings are the answer. Picks and hatchets are the tools he names.

That's what the text says, baker. “They have burned Your sanctuary to the ground.” (Psalm 74:7) First the carvings, then the whole building. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's okay to just let it be heavy.

Sealing it shut would've left the building standing, friend. Asaph says, “They have burned Your sanctuary to the ground.” (Psalm 74:7) No locks, no padlocks in this verse. It's fire, and it's about as hard as a verse gets.

The psalm never says the enemy moved in, baker. What it says is, “They have burned Your sanctuary to the ground.” (Psalm 74:7) You can't turn a pile of ashes into a fort. The sanctuary is gone, and that's the sorrow of the verse.

I can see why you'd think the damage ended at the sanctuary, baker, but Asaph says more. “They burned down every place where God met us in the land.” (Psalm 74:8) Every place, not just one. The enemy said in their hearts, “We will crush them completely,” and it shows.

False is right, friend. Asaph says, “They burned down every place where God met us in the land.” (Psalm 74:8) That's every place, with none left standing. It's a heavy line, and the whole land felt it.
Right, baker. Asaph says, “There is no longer any prophet.” (Psalm 74:9) No signs and no prophet. I think that's a very quiet kind of loneliness.
Asaph doesn't mention a king in that line, friend. He says, “There is no longer any prophet.” (Psalm 74:9) A prophet is the one missing from this verse. A king isn't named at all.
Priests aren't named in verse 9, baker. Asaph says, “There is no longer any prophet.” (Psalm 74:9) Signs are gone, and the prophet is gone with them. That's the whole list he gives.
Taunt is the word, friend. “How long, O God, will the enemy taunt You?” (Psalm 74:10) Asaph is asking out loud, right to God. He doesn't whisper it, and he doesn't pretend everything's fine.

Fear is a good word, baker, but Asaph didn't use it here. He asks, “How long, O God, will the enemy taunt You?” (Psalm 74:10) A taunt is a loud insult, so the enemy is not tiptoeing around. The word that fits the blank is taunt.
Serving would be the opposite of what's happening, friend. Asaph asks, “How long, O God, will the enemy taunt You?” (Psalm 74:10) The enemy is mocking, not serving. Taunt is the word.
True, baker. Asaph asks, “Will the foe revile Your name forever?” (Psalm 74:10) The insults aren't just about the people. They're aimed at God's own name.

I can see why you'd hesitate, friend, but this one is True. Asaph asks, “Will the foe revile Your name forever?” (Psalm 74:10) Revile means to insult, and the target is God's name. Asaph is hurting for the people and for God's name too.

explanations.answer: Stretch it out to destroy the enemy
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Asaph says, “Why do You withdraw Your strong right hand? Stretch it out to destroy them!” (Psalm 74:11) He's honest about what he wants. Nothing polite in that line, just a plain ask.

explanations.answer: Raise it up to bless the land
explanations.explanation: A nice thought, friend, but it's not what Asaph asks here. He says, “Stretch it out to destroy them!” (Psalm 74:11) The ruins and the roaring have him asking for the enemy to be stopped. Blessing the land isn't what's on his lips in this line.

Resting sounds peaceful, baker, but Asaph isn't asking for peace and quiet. He says, “Stretch it out to destroy them!” (Psalm 74:11) He wants that hand out and working. Not resting, and not tucked away.

True, friend. Right after the hard questions, Asaph says, “Yet God is my King from ancient times, working salvation on the earth.” (Psalm 74:12) He asks the tough stuff and then names who God is. Both of those live in the same prayer.

I get why you'd think so, baker, with all those hard questions. But Asaph turns and says, “Yet God is my King from ancient times, working salvation on the earth.” (Psalm 74:12) He said all of it in the same breath. So this one is True.
Leviathan, baker. Asaph says to God, “You crushed the heads of Leviathan.” (Psalm 74:14) It's a big name for a big thing, and the verse says God handled it.
Behemoth sounds big enough for the job, friend, but Asaph doesn't name it here. He says, “You crushed the heads of Leviathan.” (Psalm 74:14) Leviathan is the creature in this verse.
The great fish is a different story, baker. That one swallowed Jonah (Jonah 1:17). Here Asaph says, “You crushed the heads of Leviathan.” (Psalm 74:14)
True, friend. Asaph says to God, “You dried up the ever-flowing rivers.” (Psalm 74:15) Rivers that never stop flowing, and He dried them up. Makes me feel better about my bakery's one leaky faucet.
It sounds like too much, baker, but it's right there. Asaph says, “You dried up the ever-flowing rivers.” (Psalm 74:15) Ever-flowing rivers, dried up by God. So this one is True.
Winter, friend. Asaph says, “You made the summer and winter.” (Psalm 74:17) Both ends of the year are His. That's a lot of oven weather and a lot of cold mornings covered.

Harvest is a season word too, baker, but it's not what Asaph says. He says, “You set all the boundaries of the earth; You made the summer and winter.” (Psalm 74:17) The pair here is summer and winter, the hot and the cold.
Rain is a good guess, friend, but the verse doesn't use it. Asaph says, “You made the summer and winter.” (Psalm 74:17) Summer and winter are the pair. Rain never shows up in this line.
Spurned, baker. Asaph says, “a foolish people has spurned Your name.” (Psalm 74:18) To spurn is to turn something away with scorn. He's telling God exactly what's being done to His name.
Praise is the opposite of what Asaph says, friend. He says, “a foolish people has spurned Your name.” (Psalm 74:18) Spurned means turned away with scorn. This people is no fan club.

Fear would have been a better response, baker, but that's not what's happening. Asaph says, “a foolish people has spurned Your name.” (Psalm 74:18) Spurned means they turned it away with scorn. That's the word that fits.
His afflicted, friend. Asaph prays, “do not forget the lives of Your afflicted forever.” (Psalm 74:19) He's asking for the hurting ones by name. I think that's a prayer with a lot of love in it.
Priests don't come up in that line, baker. Asaph prays, “do not forget the lives of Your afflicted forever.” (Psalm 74:19) The afflicted are the ones he's asking about.

Kings aren't mentioned in verse 19, friend. Asaph prays, “do not forget the lives of Your afflicted forever.” (Psalm 74:19) The afflicted are the ones he's pleading for. It's the hurting, not the crowned.

Covenant is right, baker. Asaph says, “Consider Your covenant.” (Psalm 74:20) A covenant is a binding promise, and he points to it right in his prayer. He's asking God to look at what He Himself set up.
The altar isn't in that verse, friend. Asaph says, “Consider Your covenant.” (Psalm 74:20) A covenant is a binding promise God made with His people. That's what he's asking God to consider.
Festivals sound like a fun answer, baker, but Asaph doesn't name them. He says, “Consider Your covenant.” (Psalm 74:20) That's the thing God made with His people, a binding promise.

explanations.answer: Violence fills the dark places of the land
explanations.explanation: That's what the verse says, friend. “Consider Your covenant, for haunts of violence fill the dark places of the land.” (Psalm 74:20) Asaph gives the reason right in the line. It's a heavy one, so I think it's fair to say that out loud.

explanations.answer: The people have forgotten the covenant
explanations.explanation: The verse never says the people forgot, baker. Asaph says, “Consider Your covenant, for haunts of violence fill the dark places of the land.” (Psalm 74:20) The reason he gives is the violence. I'd stick with what the text says.

explanations.answer: The enemy has written a new law
explanations.explanation: No new law shows up in this psalm, friend. Asaph says, “Consider Your covenant, for haunts of violence fill the dark places of the land.” (Psalm 74:20) The reason he gives is the violence in the dark places.
Praise, baker. Asaph prays, “may the poor and needy praise Your name.” (Psalm 74:21) He asks God to put praise back in their mouths. I think that's a good prayer for anyone.

Fear is a good word, friend, but it's not what Asaph asks. He prays, “may the poor and needy praise Your name.” (Psalm 74:21) He's asking for praise, not fear. The oppressed are already carrying plenty.
Guarding is a job for a sentry, baker, and this verse isn't about that. Asaph prays, “may the poor and needy praise Your name.” (Psalm 74:21) Praise is what he wants for them.

I can see how it sounds that way, friend, since Asaph is praying for his people. But he says, “Rise up, O God; defend Your cause!” (Psalm 74:22) It's God's cause, not Israel's alone. So this one is False.
False, baker. Asaph says, “Rise up, O God; defend Your cause!” (Psalm 74:22) He calls it God's cause, not Israel's alone. Then he adds, “Remember how the fool mocks You all day long.”

That's the last line, friend. Asaph prays, “Do not disregard the clamor of Your adversaries, the uproar of Your enemies that ascends continually.” (Psalm 74:23) The noise doesn't stop, and he's laying it all before God.

No priests in that last line, baker. Asaph prays, “Do not disregard the clamor of Your adversaries, the uproar of Your enemies that ascends continually.” (Psalm 74:23) What he names is the clamor of the adversaries.

Songs would be a sweet ending, friend, but that's not what the line says. Asaph prays, “Do not disregard the clamor of Your adversaries, the uproar of Your enemies that ascends continually.” (Psalm 74:23) It's the enemies' uproar, which keeps ascending.
